scenes.title: The shadow at noon
scenes.caption: Before he sails, Pytheas sets up a gnomon at midsummer noon and measures its shadow: 120 parts of pole to 41⅘ of shadow. Hipparchus still used the figure two centuries later to fix Massalia's latitude, one of the earliest such measurements on record.

scenes.title: The tin road at low tide
scenes.caption: The people of Belerion, used to foreign merchants and friendly to strangers, dig and smelt tin, beat it into ingots shaped like knucklebones and cart them over the sand at low tide to an island called Ictis, where the traders buy it. The account in Diodorus probably goes back to Pytheas.

scenes.title: Where the sun goes to rest
scenes.caption: 'The barbarians showed us where the sun goes to rest,' Pytheas wrote, for near Thule the summer night lasts only two or three hours. Beyond, he said, was neither land nor sea nor air but a mixture of them, like a 'sea-lung', that could be neither walked on nor sailed.

scenes.title: The amber island
scenes.caption: On an island he calls Abalus, a day's sail from the coast, Pytheas says the spring tides wash up amber, which the islanders burn as fuel and sell to their neighbours the Teutones. Pliny preserves the report; the island may be Heligoland or the Jutland shore.

scenes.title: On the Ocean
scenes.caption: Home in Massalia, Pytheas writes On the Ocean. Eratosthenes and Hipparchus build on its latitudes; Polybius and Strabo call its author a liar. The book is lost, and survives only in the quotations of those who doubted it.
